newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: COCOA - Cool summer to boost Europe third qtr grind.
newsitem.headline: COCOA - Cool summer to boost Europe third qtr grind.

text.p: Cool temperatures across much of Europe this summer and a revival in chocolate demand from the east are expected to be major factors behind strong cocoa grind figures from the continent's three main chocolate producers.
Analysts said cold weather in particular has helped produce a pattern of roaring third quarter output in the Netherlands, UK and Germany. Figures are due out from the end of this week.
A warm summer in Europe can seriously dent demand for cocoa as consumers shun chocolate and cocoa-based hot drinks.
In its September cocoa market report, trade house E.D. and F Man said third quarter grindings should be strong across Europe.

"Demand for cocoa butter during the summer has been higher than last year due to cooler weather prevailing over most of western Europe. This should be reflected in in stronger third quarter grindings in the Netherlands, UK and Germany."
Grind forecasts range between a five percent jump for German processing, where there is talk of some production disruption, and a 20 percent leap in UK output, but that too is conditional.

"Business has been very good indeed, there has been very good demand for cocoa butter and liquor. Dutch factories are running at full capacity," Louis Bensdorp, president of the Dutch Cocoa Association (NCV) told Reuters.
Analysts expect the Dutch grind to rise by nearly ten percent from its third quarter 1995 figure of 85,311 tonnes. In the second quarter 1996 it jumped 6.4 percent to 90,724 tonnes.
Production in the Netherlands, the world's biggest grinder, has also been boosted by good demand from eastern Europe, where chocolate demand has started to pick up, industry sources said.
This has been helped by the historically low prices for products such as powder. "I think a lot of consumers have suddenly woken up to how cheap these are," one industry source.
Butter ratios have started to improve this quarter as a result, the nearby rates ticking up to just above 2.80.

The picture in Germany is a similar one but industry sources said problems at major grinder Hamester, which moved some of its production from Berlin to Hamburg at the start of the quarter, may dent the final figure.
"There's talk of problems with the machinery that was moved over and this could affect the German figure," one said.
"It could make the difference between a three percent increase and a five percent one," he said.
No-one at Hamester was available to comment.

In the third quarter last year, the German grind was 9.1 percent down at 61,523 tonnes, reflecting sluggish sales in the chocolate industry and the temporary shift in some production to the Netherlands. The figure bounced back in the second quarter this year, rising 5.3 percent to 59,471 tonnes.
In the UK, the grind jump in Q3 1996 is forecast to be more dramatic, mainly because last year's figure was abnormally low.
Industry sources said the rise could be as much as 20 percent up on last year's 34,400 tonnes, partly helped by the resumption of production at one major grinder.
The year-ago grindings, the worst quarter in 1995, were affected by the closure of the plant.
One UK-based analyst predicted a higher grind for the third quarter, citing perceptions of a general upturn in chocolate consumption, aided by the favourable summer.
He said the summer was less of a problem after last year's very hot one. "Chocolate demand is better this time." --Amsterdam Newsroom +31 20 504 5000
